title: Five years: the practices
hookLine: seva, kirtan, langar, simran and the gurdwara
tomorrow: one bus ride, seven prayers. which line from each does Simran keep?

lines: WHY FEED ANYBODY WHO WALKS IN?
cards: Her shoes. That's the first thing Maya notices: a wall of shoes at the door, sneakers next to work boots next to tiny sandals. Then the scarf Simran hands her for her hair.
Then the hall downstairs, people sitting in long rows on the floor, a volunteer coming down the line with a pitcher of water. Nobody asks Maya who she is. Somebody just puts a plate in front of her.
On the drive home she has one question. Why do they feed anybody who walks in?

teach.b: Simran's answer is the whole list of practices, because they hold each other up. Seva, service with no pay, is who cooked the dal and who'll wash the pots. Kirtan is the hymns being sung upstairs.
Simran, the practice her name comes from, is the Name kept in mind while the hands work. The gurdwara is the door that opens on all of it.
And langar is the meal, but the point is the row. Everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food, whoever they are.
Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the langar before they came to see him, and that even an emperor sat in the row. Here's where a neighbor tradition says something close.

In the Letter to the Hebrews, Christians read: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Both say the stranger at the door gets fed. That's the shared ground.

teach.h: ONE REASON IN THE GUEST, ONE IN THE FLOOR.
teach.b: And an honest difference: the Hebrews line gives a reason in the guest, some guests have been angels. Langar puts its reason in the seating.
Nobody is higher on the floor than anybody else. Maya thinks about it at a red light. Then she says the dal was really good, and could she come back.

how: Gurdwaras keep a langar, a free kitchen run by volunteers, where anyone may eat; guests remove their shoes and cover their heads, and the meal is usually eaten sitting in rows on the floor.

games.q: the practices, and a neighbor's line — tap the pairs.
p: one row, one meal, anyone welcome

s: langar is a meal for Sikhs, or for people in need
it's for anyone who walks in, and everyone sits in the same rows and eats the same food.
tradition says Guru Amar Das asked visitors to eat in the langar first
even an emperor, the story goes, sat in the row.
the Letter to the Hebrews tells Christians to welcome strangers
be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares.

games.q: your school's culture night plans a reserved table up front for the principal and donors. what would langar's row suggest?
o: one row for everyone: same food, same level, nobody seated higher.
a reserved table is fine, as long as the food is free for everybody.
skip the meal and give a speech about equality instead.
games.why: langar's point is the seating: whoever you are, you sit on the same floor and eat the same food. free food alone isn't the whole idea.

practice: Choose the one practice you've actually kept: a line of kirtan hummed, Waheguru on the breath, or a small act of service you can do right where you are. Do two unhurried minutes of it now, small and real.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the practices, and a row on the floor where nobody sits higher. Maya wants to come back.
